title: Big Tech claims voters’ AI backlash is “anti-Trump” not “anti-tech”
gist: In the 2026 US midterms, 38 of 44 tracked data-center restriction measures passed and Democrats won governorships in Texas, Arizona, Georgia and Ohio, putting roughly 13 GW of Texas capacity and up to two-thirds of 2028 US data-center capacity at risk of delay. Tech trade group Chamber of Progress frames the result as an anti-Trump wave rather than an anti-tech mandate, while polls show 3 in 4 voters oppose data centers and analysts warn delays could benefit China.

insights.claim: Polling firm Redbud Consulting tracked 44 ballot measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers in the 2026 midterms, and 38 passed, including dozens of moratoriums and bans.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Local permitting risk for data centers has become a broad, multi-state electoral reality rather than isolated NIMBY fights.
insights.locator: One resource from a polling firm

insights.claim: Analysts expect the newly passed data-center restrictions to spare projects already under construction or approved through 2027 and instead hit future projects planned for 2028.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Near-term AI capex and supplier orders look insulated, but the 2028 capacity pipeline carries new execution risk.
insights.locator: One resource from a polling firm

insights.claim: The only ballot measure that allowed a data center to proceed, in a North Dakota city, still required developers to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings for new or expanded projects.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Even approvals now come with added cost and process, raising the baseline cost of siting data centers.

themes.theme: Texas governor upset and capacity at risk

insights.claim: Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor race, a state expected to account for more than 41% of added US data-center capacity in 2028, and she plans to delay projects until laws on water, electricity, air and property rights pass.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The single largest growth market for AI data centers now has a governor openly committed to pausing new builds.
insights.locator: Most notably, Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa

insights.claim: Bloomberg reported that approximately 13 GW of Texas data-center capacity is now exposed to Hinojosa's planned delays, a scenario developers describe as the worst case.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Quantifies the capacity at risk for hyperscalers, power developers and equipment suppliers concentrated in Texas.
insights.locator: Now, Hinojosa plans to delay projects

insights.claim: GLJ Research's Gordon Johnson expects Texas projects that already have power, permits and steel to proceed, while those with power but no state environmental permits slip 12 to 18 months, with some possibly relocating to Louisiana or Georgia.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Provides a framework to sort Texas projects by permit status and estimate a 12-18 month revenue delay for unpermitted ones.
insights.quote: those with power but no state environmental permits slip 12 to 18 months
insights.locator: Now, Hinojosa plans to delay projects

insights.claim: PIMCO's head of public policy Libby Cantrill expects more friction in the AI buildout even without statewide moratoria, through longer permitting timelines and more concessions demanded of data-center developers.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A major bond manager sees structurally slower and costlier data-center development regardless of outright bans.
insights.quote: we expect to see a lot more sand in the gears of the AI buildout regardless
insights.locator: Now, Hinojosa plans to delay projects

insights.claim: Democrats also won governor races in Arizona, Georgia and Ohio, the next three biggest states courting data centers, and Axios projected nearly two-thirds of 2028 US data-center capacity could face Texas-style delays.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The policy risk is national, not limited to Texas, threatening the majority of planned 2028 AI capacity.
insights.locator: Big Tech downplays AI election results

insights.claim: Bloomberg estimated that half of US data centers are now more vulnerable to scrutiny, and developers will likely face tighter limits on tax incentives and stronger rules on who pays for grid infrastructure and water use, raising costs.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Loss of tax incentives and cost-sharing mandates would compress returns on data-center investment.

insights.claim: Gartner recently estimated the AI boom is nearly $5 trillion short of paying for itself, so construction delays that push back revenue are especially damaging for AI firms.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Delays add pressure to an AI investment cycle already questioned on returns.

themes.theme: Competing interpretations of the AI election

insights.claim: Chamber of Progress CEO and former Google executive Adam Kovacevich argued the results show little evidence of a mandate to crack down on AI, noting Democratic gubernatorial candidates who opposed data-center bans won at a higher rate than those who supported them.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The industry will lobby that the mandate is economic, not anti-AI, shaping how aggressively new officials act.
insights.quote: Let’s not confuse an anti-Trump wave with an anti-tech mandate.

insights.claim: NBC News exit polls showed 3 in 4 voters oppose data centers and more than half said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, though cost of living and corruption ranked higher.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Data-center opposition is now a mainstream voting issue, making political support for AI buildouts costly.
insights.locator: Poll: 3 out of 4 voters

insights.claim: Analysts told Axios that voters seemed more concerned about efforts to block state AI regulation than about data centers, and in four swing districts voters trusted Democrats over Republicans by 7 to 10 points to hold AI executives accountable.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Federal preemption of state AI rules is politically weakened, raising odds of a patchwork of state AI regulation.

insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Bipartisan local hostility means siting risk persists regardless of which party holds power.

insights.claim: Natixis senior economist Gary Ng Cheuk-yan argues a Democrat-controlled Congress constraining US computing capacity would keep US AI token prices high, letting China export cost-effective inference services backed by abundant electricity.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: US compute scarcity could sustain inference pricing for US providers while opening export opportunities for Chinese AI.

insights.claim: Lombard Odier CIO Michael Strobaek noted Trump can still veto federal laws, so Democrats would need substantial Republican support for new AI rules, though a majority could block rollbacks of EPA protections aimed at aiding data centers.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Federal AI legislation is likely gridlocked; the more realistic impact is on environmental deregulation for data centers.

insights.claim: Elon Musk spent almost half a billion dollars on Republican candidates through October, the largest individual donation in the 2026 midterms, and SpaceX and Tesla shares fell as results came in amid doubts about a potential merger of the two.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Musk's political exposure is now a direct risk factor for SpaceX/Tesla valuation and any combination plans.
